blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the remarkable success of Let's Encrypt as the world's largest HTTPS Certificate Authority (CA), accounting for more valid certificates than all other browser-trusted CAs combined. He emphasizes two key achievements: first, Let's Encrypt made the web more secure by prioritizing ease-of-use, breaking the typical trade-off between security and usability. Second, it established a sustainable funding model for an open-source project and free online service, avoiding the burnout of small benefactor-maintained initiatives. The blog post details Let's Encrypt's rapid growth since its launch in 2015, its fully automated end-to-end service, and its integration with hosting and CDN providers. Colyer also notes the significant impact of Let's Encrypt's shorter certificate lifetimes (90 days) in reducing expired certificate incidents. The paper delves into the technical and organizational challenges overcome to achieve this success, including the development of the ACME protocol and the Boulder CA software stack.
paper_title: Let's Encrypt: An automated certificate authority to encrypt the entire web
paper_abstract: 1 Let’s Encrypt is a free, open, and automated HTTPS certificate authority (CA) created to advance HTTPS adoption to the entire Web. Since its launch in late 2015, Let’s Encrypt has grown to become the world’s largest HTTPS CA, accounting for more currently valid certificates than all other browser-trusted CAs combined. By January 2019, it had issued over 538 million certificates for 223 million domain names. We describe how we built Let’s Encrypt, including the architecture of the CA software system (Boulder) and the structure of the organization that operates it (ISRG), and we discuss lessons learned from the experience. We also describe the design of ACME, the IETF-standard protocol we created to automate CA–server interactions and certificate issuance, and survey the diverse ecosystem of ACME clients, including Certbot, a software agent we created to automate HTTPS deployment. Finally, we measure Let’s Encrypt’s impact on the Web and the CA ecosystem. We hope that the success of Let’s Encrypt can provide a model for further enhancements to the Web PKI and for future Internet security infrastructure. HTTPS [78] is the cryptographic foundation of the Web, providing an encrypted and authenticated form of HTTP over the TLS transport [79]. When HTTPS was introduced by Netscape twenty-five years ago [51], the primary use cases were protecting financial transactions and login credentials, but users today face a growing range of threats from hostile networks—including mass surveillance and censorship by governments [99, 106], consumer profiling and ad injection by ISPs [30, 95], and insertion of malicious code by network devices [68]—which make HTTPS important for practically every Web request. Many cryptographic flaws in TLS have been discovered and mitigated (e.g., [11, 13, 17, 23, 37, 69]), but low adoption of HTTPS posed an even starker risk: as recently as 2015, 55–70% of browser page loads used plaintext HTTP [47].
